articles.title: Google’s Pixel 11 phone preorders come with up to $350 in gift cards
articles.summary: Google has officially unveiled the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, and Pixel 11 Fold. They’re available for preorder from retailers and carriers.
articles.body: Looking to get your hands on the latest Pixel devices? After weeks of leaks and rumors, Google has officially announced its next generation of Pixel phones and watches. The base Pixel 11 starts at $899, the Pro and Pro XL are $1,099 and $1,299 respectively, and the Pro Fold starts at $1,899. The watch comes in two sizes, with the smaller 41mm model starting at $399, and the larger 45mm model starting at $429. The phones are available for preorder now, and will ship on August 20th, 2026. If you’re looking to preorder an unlocked phone on its own, your main options are Best Buy, Amazon, and directly from the Google Store. All three are running a similar introductory deal, where you’ll receive a gift card for a future purchase at that retailer, with the value depending on which model you buy. The Pixel 11 includes a $100 gift card, the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL include a $200 gift card, and the Pixel 11 Pro Fold includes a $350 gift card. Only Google lists an end date for the promotion, which is August 27th, 2026. If you’d also like a Pixel Watch 5, Google and Amazon will give you additional credit towards that purchase instead of the gift card. The Pixel 11 and 41mm watch bundle is $1,168.99, effectively a $130 discount if you bought the two devices separately, but only in obsidian. The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL with a 41mm watch as a bundle is discounted by $250. The Amazon bundles include only the Wi-Fi versions of the Pixel Watch 5 and only in limited color combinations. The Google store will let you apply the credit to other in-stock variants. If you buy a Pixel 11 Pro Fold, you can opt for a 41mm Wi-Fi watch for free, with Amazon offering obsidian only and Google letting you choose your colors. Each phone is powered by the new Tensor G6 processor, which Google says is capable of 25 percent faster web browsing and 15 percent improvement to app loading speeds over the Tensor G5. The camera and video features are a focus of the new Pixel 11 series phones. The new Magic Capture feature lets you forget about snapping a great shot, and instead stitches together a series of clips and photos from a longer video. All four phones also featuring upgraded batteries and fast charging, with wireless charging support for Qi2.2 up to 25W. If you’re deciding which Pixel is right for you, make sure to check out our initial hands-on impressions for the new Pixel 11 series phones and the Pixel Watch 5. Where to preorder the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL The Pixel 11 Pro starts at $1,099 for the base model with 256GB of storage, and goes up to $1,219 for the 512GB model, or $1,449 for the 1TB model. The larger Pixel 11 Pro XL starts at $1,299 for the 256GB configuration, with the 512GB costing $1,419 and the 1TB model priced at $1,649. For both phones, the 256GB version has 12GB of memory, while the larger capacity models have 16GB of memory. The phones are available in four colors: canyon, fog, olive, and obsidian. For cameras, the Pixel 11 sports a 48MP sensor wide camera, a 13MP ultrawide, a 10.8 MP telephoto with 5x optical zoom, and a 10.5MP selfie camera with a 95 degree field of view. The same deal is available for a Pixel 11 Pro XL with qualified trade-ins. If you’re starting a new line and buying a device that’s $500 or more with an installment plan, you can also claim 50 percent off a Pixel Watch 5. Update, August 12th: Added additional deal details.

articles.title: Pixel 11 event live blog: Let’s watch Trevor Noah introduce Google’s new phones
articles.summary: Follow our live blog of Google’s Pixel 11 launch event, which will be hosted by Trevor Noah and feature Steph Curry and other celebrities. The show kicks off at 6PM ET.
articles.body: It’s almost time for the Made by Google keynote, where the company will show off the brand-new Pixel hardware it announced today. Like last year, it’ll be a celebrity-packed live show, though Trevor Noah is hosting instead of Jimmy Fallon. If the 2025 show was any indication, today’s broadcast might be something of a cringefest. If you’ve been following tech news this morning, you already know a lot about the new Pixels. Press and creators were able to publish extensive hands-on impressions of the new hardware hours ago, and you can read our coverage of the Pixel 11 phones, their new camera features, the Pixel Watch 5, and more right now. Google could pull something unexpected out of a hat. But it seems more likely that this show isn’t for the people who devour every hands-on the moment they’re published. Instead, the event is likely intended to reach a more mainstream audience that might watch the livestream after work or as a replay at a later time. Victoria Song will be there in person, while the rest of us will be watching remotely, and we’ll all be blogging all of our secondhand embarrassment right here. Things kick off at 6PM ET / 3PM PT. You can watch the event on the embedded YouTube video while following along with our live thoughts below. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c84y9gAY90c]

articles.summary:

articles.title: Who really needs a cocktail robot?
articles.summary: Bartesian's cocktail makers would be best described like a Keurig or Nespresso machine, but for alcoholic drinks.
articles.body:
Bartesian’s cocktail makers would be best described like a Keurig or Nespresso machine, but for alcoholic drinks. The Bartesian Duet model that I tested certainly lives up to that description — it’s really easy to serve a bunch of different cocktails with the push of a button, plus your own liquor.

But as I sipped on my raspberry ginger gimlet, I couldn’t shake the nagging question: Who is actually going to buy a $300 cocktail robot?

There’s nothing wrong with the product. And it does exactly what it says! In the sleekly designed machine, you add your spirits of choice (between one and four types of liquor, depending on which model you’re using) and plop in a Bartesian capsule with hyper-concentrated mixes for multi-ingredient drinks like espresso martinis, watermelon margaritas, mai tais, and cosmos. There’s a barcode on the capsule that your machine scans to determine which spirit (or spirits) you need in your drink, and then you can select how strong you want your drink to be, which modulates the amount of water the machine will use to dilute the concentrate. Then, you put the drink in the provided, high-quality cocktail shaker with some ice to cool it down before pouring it into your glass.

When I invited some friends over to test the Bartesian, we enjoyed the inherent novelty of trying out a product we’d never seen or used before. Once we all sat down with our various drinks, we tried to decide who actually makes up the target audience for such an odd product, which also requires the purchase of cocktail capsules at about $2.50 each.

The Bartesian is not for true cocktail lovers — the capsules don’t actually contain any alcohol, which means that if you’re making a drink like an aviation, you’re getting some sort of non-alcoholic approximation of ingredients like crème de violette and maraschino liqueur.

It’s no coincidence that my friends and I all liked the Bartesian’s lemon drop capsules the best, since the only alcoholic ingredient in the drink is the vodka that we bought ourselves to add to the machine. To be fair to Bartesian, it’s not like you’d recommend a Nespresso machine to your friend who owns a Fellow kettle and only buys single-origin beans.

This cocktail robot is also not for anyone who is even remotely worried about the amount of counter space in their kitchen. It’s pretty big for something that you (hopefully?) aren’t using on a daily basis, and if anything, it would probably encourage me to start drinking more often just to justify the $300 expense (or $199.99 if you buy it during Amazon’s current limited time deal ). Plus, if you have counter space to spare, you probably have a lot of money. And if you have a lot of money and like cocktails, I’d say you are more likely to have a fully stocked bar with fancy liqueurs already. What will the other partners at your law firm say if you serve aviations that don’t use real crème de violette?

Even as someone who thinks Tito’s is top-shelf liquor (I am not that fancy), I could tell that something tasted a little bit artificial about most of these drinks. My friends and I all doctored up our drinks with some seltzer and lemon juice, which made them taste much better. But this kind of post-robot mixing sort of defeats the point of the whole endeavor.

Maybe my tastes just don’t align with the mixologists at Bartesian — my colleague Lauren reviewed a different Bartesian unit last year and told me that she loved it , especially the margaritas.

Drink preferences aside, I still keep coming back to the same question: Who is this product for?

I could see the Bartesian being useful if you host a lot of parties and don’t hire a bartender, since you can make a whole cocktail menu’s worth of drinks without much effort or planning. One friend remarked that this machine feels like the sort of thing that an older couple would keep in their beach house to impress their friends. A colleague suggested that this could really shine in a retirement home. Personally, I could see a Bartesian at a coworking space’s happy hour, where people are just happy to get free drinks… then again, there’s a reason why WeWork stopped offering unlimited beer back in the day.

This post originally published August 13 and has been updated with new pricing information.

articles.title: Google’s best new camera feature is only for the Pixel 11 series
articles.summary: Google’s Camera Looks feature will only be available for the Pixel 11 lineup, the company confirms to The Verge.
articles.body: Arguably the coolest new photo feature for the Pixel 11 lineup is Google’s new Camera Looks, which process image data differently at the sensor level to produce photos that don’t have that “smartphone” look. The result is new styles like “Digi,” which mimics the style of photos taken by older digital cameras. But to use Camera Looks, at least initially, you’ll need to have one of Google’s Pixel 11 phones. “Our latest camera updates are only available on our latest devices,” Google spokesperson Alex Moriconi tells The Verge. “We’re always looking to bring experiences to more users, but have nothing to share at this time.” That last sentence leaves some wiggle room for Camera Looks to come to older Pixel phones at some point in the future, though it’s unclear if or when that might actually happen. If you want to learn more about how the Camera Looks feature works, check out David’s big article, which features an interview with Isaac Reynolds, the head of the Pixel camera team.

articles.title: We’re reaching peak camera with the Sony A7R VI
articles.summary: The Sony A7R VI is a 66.8-megapixel spec monster of a mirrorless camera. With a fully stacked sensor and 30fps blackout-free shooting, the old compromises of high-resolution cameras are long gone.
articles.body: It wasn’t long ago that shooting with a super high-resolution camera meant making serious sacrifices for the sake of all those megapixels. Enter the A7R VI. Sony’s latest flagship high-res camera is a 66.8-megapixel spec monster. In addition to its modest bump in resolution from the last-gen A7R V, it uses a new sensor and processor that unlock nearly any kind of shooting — from sports and action to usable 8K video. It’s a huge departure from years ago, when high-resolution cameras were slower, noisier, and more specialized as a result of all those megapixels.  The A7R VI’s fully stacked sensor and new Bionz XR2 processor allow it to shoot full-resolution bursts at up to 30 frames per second without any viewfinder blackout. And that faster sensor means there’s little downside to using the electronic shutter full time, meaning you get truly silent shooting for any moment you want to be stealthy. The A7R VI also has 8.5 stops of in-body image stabilization, dual USB-C ports (because why not), and Sony’s new AI-based autofocus system. [Product: Sony A7R VI | https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bhphotovideo.com%2Fc%2Fproduct%2F1970580-REG%2Fsony_ilce7rm6b_a7r_vi_mirrorless_camera.html, https://adorama.prf.hn/click/camref:1100l5pDsF/[p_id:1011l394533]/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.adorama.com%2Fsony-alpha-a7r-vi-mirrorless-camera%2Fp%2Fisoa7r6%2F, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/8836598/type/dlg/https://electronics.sony.com/imaging/interchangeable-lens-cameras/full-frame/p/ilce7rm6b] The A7R V was pretty quick, shooting 60-megapixel images at up to 10 frames per second with its mechanical shutter, but the A7R VI pumps out its 9984 x 6656 resolution RAW files lightning-fast. And these files are huge. They average about 60 megabytes in lossless compressed RAW format, so that one-second burst of 30 shots can soak up 1.8GB. Wild. I already use a pretty high-res Sony camera that shoots fast: the original A1. I pair it with the even faster but much lower-res A9 III for my wedding photo gigs. But even though I’m used to Sony’s speedy shooters, the A7R VI’s over-the-top resolution and flexibility really impressed me. In the past, super high-res cameras were reserved for studio work, but the A7R VI blows away any reservations over using a camera with 60-plus megapixels of resolution on just about anything: landscapes, sports, action, photojournalism, street photography, portraits, etc. It. Does. Everything. time I used it for casual snapshots, family weekend trips (including a mini safari), Verge product images, and a freelance wedding shoot (as the second photographer). I quickly realized that despite its new battery and ever-so-slightly revised grip around it, the A7R VI feels just like the A7R V — and therefore a whole lot like nearly any other A7 camera. And this is in a $4,500 camera, compared to the newer version of my camera, which currently costs $7,000. This is the first of Sony’s R cameras I’ve looked at and thought, “Yeah, this could be my one camera for everything.” (If I wanted that and if I only needed one camera, of course.) It does much of what I need from my A1 and A9 III at a higher resolution and a lower price. Camera tech is constantly improving, but it will probably be a while before any camera — from Sony or anyone else — is superior enough to justify an upgrade from here. Photography by Antonio G. paragraphs: It wasn’t long ago that shooting with a super high-resolution camera meant making serious sacrifices for the sake of all those megapixels. Enter the A7R VI. Sony’s latest flagship high-res camera is a 66.8-megapixel spec monster. In addition to its modest bump in resolution from the last-gen A7R V, it uses a new sensor and processor that unlock nearly any kind of shooting — from sports and action to usable 8K video. It’s a huge departure from years ago, when high-resolution cameras were slower, noisier, and more specialized as a result of all those megapixels.  The A7R VI’s fully stacked sensor and new Bionz XR2 processor allow it to shoot full-resolution bursts at up to 30 frames per second without any viewfinder blackout. And that faster sensor means there’s little downside to using the electronic shutter full time, meaning you get truly silent shooting for any moment you want to be stealthy. The A7R VI also has 8.5 stops of in-body image stabilization, dual USB-C ports (because why not), and Sony’s new AI-based autofocus system. [Product: Sony A7R VI | https://go.skimresources.com/?id=1025X1701640&xs=1&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bhphotovideo.com%2Fc%2Fproduct%2F1970580-REG%2Fsony_ilce7rm6b_a7r_vi_mirrorless_camera.html, https://adorama.prf.hn/click/camref:1100l5pDsF/[p_id:1011l394533]/destination:https%3A%2F%2Fwww.adorama.com%2Fsony-alpha-a7r-vi-mirrorless-camera%2Fp%2Fisoa7r6%2F, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/8836598/type/dlg/https://electronics.sony.com/imaging/interchangeable-lens-cameras/full-frame/p/ilce7rm6b] The A7R V was pretty quick, shooting 60-megapixel images at up to 10 frames per second with its mechanical shutter, but the A7R VI pumps out its 9984 x 6656 resolution RAW files lightning-fast. And these files are huge. They average about 60 megabytes in lossless compressed RAW format, so that one-second burst of 30 shots can soak up 1.8GB. Wild. I already use a pretty high-res Sony camera that shoots fast: the original A1. I pair it with the even faster but much lower-res A9 III for my wedding photo gigs. But even though I’m used to Sony’s speedy shooters, the A7R VI’s over-the-top resolution and flexibility really impressed me. In the past, super high-res cameras were reserved for studio work, but the A7R VI blows away any reservations over using a camera with 60-plus megapixels of resolution on just about anything: landscapes, sports, action, photojournalism, street photography, portraits, etc. It. Does. Everything. articles.title: Xteink’s tiny e-readers are getting access to free books through Libby
articles.summary: Xteink’s pocket-friendly e-readers are even more appealing with access to DRM-protected ebooks from Libby and Kobo.
articles.body: One of the big tradeoffs with Xteink’s pocket-friendly e-readers is a lack of easy access to ebooks. On a Kindle or Kobo you can download tens of thousands of titles through each device’s respective online bookstores, but with Xteink’s devices you have to source DRM-free ebooks on your own. That’s about to change, as the developers of CrossPoint Reader, a free alternative firmware for the X3, X4, and X4 Pro, are introducing support for third-party plug-ins that will expand the e-readers’ capabilities. One of the first from the community will give the devices access to DRM-protected ebooks borrowed through OverDrive’s Libby library app, or purchased through bookstores like Kobo’s. The new functionality is still in beta, but while the team behind CrossPoint Reader provided me with custom firmware I’ve been testing on the X4 Pro for the past few days, it’s now available to anyone who wants to try it. Getting ebooks from Libby onto the tiny e-readers isn’t as streamlined as using its mobile app or as simple as Kobo’s native OverDrive support, but it’s much easier than I expected. If you’re already comfortable with wirelessly transferring files to your tiny e-reader, loading ebooks from Libby isn’t much harder. [Image: Until now, you had to source DRM-free ebooks to load and read on Xteink’s e-readers. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/xteinklibby2.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The first step is saying good riddance to the frustrating stock firmware on Xteink’s devices and installing the free CrossPoint Reader alternative. The easiest approach is to connect your e-reader to your computer with its USB-C cable, power it on, and then flash the new firmware directly through a browser using the CrossPoint Reader website that lets you select your specific device and which version of the firmware you want. You then need to download and install CrossPoint Reader’s new Plugin Store, which is available here. Installation is as simple as unzipping a few files onto your e-reader’s microSD card, which will put a new Plugins section on the e-reader’s homescreen. It’s currently populated with a few different tools you can download, but the important one to install is the “Protected Content” plug-in. It runs through CrossPoint Reader’s built-in web server (which is probably much easier to use than you think) and allows Xteink’s devices to access ebooks protected by the Adobe Digital Editions DRM. To get it all working you’ll need a free ByteBooks account (or you can convert an older Adobe Digital Editions account you haven’t touched in years) so you can login and authorize your e-reader to open DRM-protected ebooks. You’ll also need access to Libby itself on another device, which requires a library card to sign in. For several reasons, including the fact that Xteink’s devices use low-power ESP-32 processors, you’re not able to search or download ebooks from Libby directly on the e-readers themselves. [Image: You can use CrossPoint Reader’s built-in web server to wirelessly copy ebooks to your e-reader. But its new “Protected Content” plug-in now allows you to load DRM-protected ebooks, too. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/xteinklibby4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Once you borrow a book the Libby apps will let you download it as a protected EPUB file. What you’re actually downloading first is a tiny ACSM file that an authorized reading app uses to access the DRM-protected ebook file. The new “Protected Content” plug-in running through the CrossPoint Reader web server processes an ACSM file moved to the microSD card, downloads a copy of the book, and copies the EPUB file to your e-reader, where you can read it for as long as the loan allows. The process is similar for ebooks purchased from stores like Kobo’s that use the EPUB format with ADE. (Amazon doesn’t.) When logged into Kobo’s website (not the desktop app) you can download an ACSM file for a book you’ve purchased, copy it to your Xteink device, and then process it with the plug-in to access the ebook you can actually read. [Image: Common Stacks is a free mobile and desktop app that streamlines the process of borrowing library books through Libby and getting them onto Xteink’s e-readers. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/xteinklibby3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] If you want to simplify the Libby process, you can instead download and install an app called Common Stacks (available for Android, Windows, and macOS, with iOS support coming soon) that’s designed to provide access to multiple free ebook libraries, including ones you host yourself. The app includes full access to Libby and can both download and send ebook files directly to Xteink’s e-readers with just a couple of clicks. Common Stacks also relies on CrossPoint Reader’s web server functionality running in the back end, but getting borrowed books onto the X4 Pro was as easy as borrowing library books on my Kobo is. While Libby and Common Stacks is one of the best ways to get free ebooks onto Xteink’s devices, you’ll want to be mindful that selection will vary from library to library, and you may occasionally have to wait to download a popular title depending on how many digital copies are available or are already loaned out. However, now that Xteink’s tiny e-readers finally have access to DRM-protected ebooks — whether borrowed or bought — they’re an even more tempting alternative to Kindles and Kobos. articles.title: 7 desk gadgets that can make your workday better
articles.summary: The right desk gadgets can help you reduce clutter, stay focused, and add a little extra convenience to your day.
articles.body:
We spend dozens of hours at our desks each week (if not more), so it’s worth creating a workspace that’s productive and enjoyable. The right desk gadgets can help you reduce clutter, stay focused, and add a little extra convenience to your day.

From ambient lighting to smart mugs, there are a lot of products designed to make the time you spend at your desk better, so we’ve combined a list of some options. Whether you’re working from home or in an office, these gadgets can help transform your workspace.

The Anker Nano Charging Station combines plugs, USB-C, and USB-A ports with retractable charging cables into a single compact charger. The station has a 1.3-inch LCD screen that displays real-time power output and temperature.

You can charge a laptop, phone, tablet, earbuds, and other devices on the same station, getting off the need for multiple chargers around your workspace. The retractable cables make it easy to plug in a device when needed without cluttering up your desk with extra wires.

The white model is available with $10 off for Prime Members at Amazon .

Logitech Lift Vertical Ergonomic Wireless Mouse — $80

If you’re working at your desk all day, a standard mouse can be hard on your wrist. The Logitech Lift Vertical Mouse is designed to promote a more natural posture in the forearm. It’s a good fit for small to medium hands, and there’s also a left-handed option available.

The vertical mouse has six customizable buttons that offer quick access to shortcuts, and connects wirelessly via Bluetooth or with the included USB receiver.

The Odistar desktop vacuum is an affordable option for keeping your desk clean and crumb-free, especially if you often eat meals at your desk. You can also use it to clean your keyboard and remove dust and debris between keys.

It’s quiet and simple to use, and because it’s so compact, you can keep it on your desk or tuck it away in a drawer until you need it. It’s cordless and uses two AA batteries. At just $13 , the desktop vacuum is a great way to keep your desk clean as you work.

If you’re someone who enjoys hot coffee but often finds yourself drinking it cold after getting sidetracked while working, the Ember Mug 2 can help keep your drinks at the perfect temperature.

You can set an exact temperature using your phone and the smart mug maintains it for up to one and a half hours with the 10-ounce version and up to 80 minutes with the 12-ounce version. The mug allows for a more consistent coffee experience, making your workday more enjoyable.

The Amazon Echo Dot can be a great addition to your work desk as you can use voice commands to set reminders, create to-do lists, check your calendar, play music, adjust smart lights, or get quick answers to questions without having to reach for your phone.

Because it’s small, you can easily place it anywhere on your desk where it can act as a hands-free assistant that helps keep you organized and focused throughout your workday.

The Govee Glide Hexa Light Panels are a simple and fun way to add some personality to your work desk setup without taking up any actual desk space. The hexagon-shaped panels mount on the wall behind your monitor and can display different colors and customizable lighting effects through the Govee app .

They can be used to create a focused atmosphere during work hours and can be switched to more dynamic effects when gaming or taking a break. The panels can be arranged in different patterns to match your style.

If you’re someone who hasn’t yet delved into the world of fidget toys but often finds yourself playing with random objects or even wrappers during calls or meetings, Speks might be for you. They’re tiny magnets that you can fidget or build with to keep your brain focused and your hands busy.

Instead of fidgeting with whatever happens to be within reach, you can have something that is actually made for the job and is more satisfying to have in your hands. They can help you stay focused and relieve stress throughout your workday.

This post originally published July 5 and has been updated with additional products.

articles.title: Fairphone is launching its latest repairable phone in the US too | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The Fairphone 6+ is a midrange Android offering, but given the increasing prices of consumer gadgets amid the ongoing component shortages, a repairable device that can be made to last for years may prove a good proposition.
articles.body:
Fairphone, the Dutch company known for its sustainable and repair-friendly phones, on Tuesday said its latest smartphone, Fairphone (Gen 6+), is now available in the U.S., starting at $649.

The company previously had a partnership with French open source operating system maker e/OS to sell a “de-Googled” version of its previous smartphones in the States, but this is the first time people in the U.S. can buy the company’s phones directly without any modifications. The company said the Fairphone 6+ will support T-Mobile and AT&T at launch.

The Fairphone 6+ is strictly a midrange Android offering, but given the increasing prices of consumer gadgets amid the ongoing component shortages, a repairable device that can be made to last for years may prove a good proposition.

“We’re delivering a device built from the ground up to be opened, repaired, and kept alive for many years,” Fairphone CEO Raymond van Eck said.

The Fairphone 6+ runs on Qualcomm’s midrange Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor and has 12GB of RAM. The phone has a 4,415 maAh battery with support for 30 W fast-charging. It features a 6.31 LTPO OLED display with an adaptive refresh rate of up to 120 Hz.

As for photography, the phone’s main camera has a 50-megapixel Sony sensor with an f/1.88 aperture, and the secondary camera has a 13-megapixel ultrawide sensor with an f/2.2 aperture. The selfie camera on the front is a 32-megapixel sensor with an f/2.0 aperture.

Personally, I would have preferred a telephoto camera instead of an ultrawide for a two-camera setup. On paper, these cameras look like they would be good enough to take photos in the daylight, but in low light, expect the performance to dwindle.

The Fairphone’s 12 replaceable parts are the main selling points, however. These include important components like the battery, cameras, USB-C port, and the display, which can be swapped out using a single screwdriver. The company offers five years of warranty and software support until 2033.

Fairphone claims it also focuses on keeping its manufacturing process sustainable. The company said it was able to reduce the carbon footprint to 30 kg of CO2e for each Fairphone 6+ it manufactured.

The Fairphone 6+ is available in Forest Green, Horizon Black, and Cobalt Blue. The company is also selling accessories like a finger loop, lanyard, and card holder, which users can install by removing the back cover.

articles.title: Apple's new macOS update reportedly contains a video of AirPods with a camera | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A video in a macOS Tahoe release candidate version shows a user wearing AirPods, looking at a book, and talking to Siri.
articles.body:
Apple seems to be preparing launch materials for its upcoming AirPods with a camera, a leaked video in the latest macOS update spotted by MacRumors suggests.

The video, found in macOS 26.7 RC, shows a man holding up a book and talking with Siri about it using visual information.

“With Visual Intelligence, your world becomes savable. See something you like? Just ask me to save it for later,” the voiceover in the video says.

MacRumors reports that these new AirPods have a camera that can be used to examine objects in front of the user and answer questions about it. The publication apparently found a line in the software code that suggests the AirPods will notify you if your hair or something else is covering the camera.

In May, Bloomberg reported that Apple was in the late stages of testing such a device. The report said the camera-equipped AirPods would look like the AirPods Pro 3, but will have a longer stem and an LED light to indicate that data is being sent to the cloud.

Other devices, like the Ray-Ban Meta Glasses, Looki pendant, and smart glasses from Rokid , already do something similar. This might be Apple’s move to embed real-world intelligence into devices before it launches smart glasses of its own.

Bloomberg noted that Apple wanted to release the new AirPods in the first half of 2026, but now that it will ship the new Siri in September, it will look to launch them along with the operating system updates.

articles.title: Tesla is finally launching the Cybercab — let’s hope it’s ready
articles.summary: Tesla is getting ready to launch its Cybercabs as part of its Robotaxi service. But the driverless vehicle’s software raises a lot of safety questions.
articles.body: The Tesla Cybercab, that golden two-seater central to Elon Musk’s robo-supremacist ambitions, is finally nearing its public launch. Whether or not the no-steering wheel and no-pedal vehicle is actually ready for public roads, let alone customers, remains very much in doubt. According to The Information, Tesla is planning a public launch of the Cybercab in Austin, Texas, as soon as this month. The driverless vehicle has been popping up around the country, although often with a steering wheel and pedals, as employees are continuing to gather data. Tesla employees have been testing the fully driverless version on private roads around the company’s campus since July. And it recently completed a training with first responders in Austin, teaching them how to move the vehicles in the event of an emergency, Brad Cesak, a spokesperson for the city of Austin, confirmed. Tesla’s Robotaxi account on X recently confirmed that a “Cybercab launch event” was imminent, inviting followers to take a ride in the company’s Model Y robotaxis in order to win a ticket. [Media: https://twitter.com/robotaxi/status/2089512069519577544] But given what we know about Tesla’s autonomous driving project so far, the Cybercab could be heading for trouble. The Cybercab operates using Tesla’s Full Self-Driving (Supervised) software, which the company claims is significantly safer than human driving. However, independent safety experts and federal regulators have called into question this claim, noting that FSD requires constant driver oversight and remains under active investigation by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration for traffic compliance failures. Over a year after its launch, Tesla’s Robotaxi service still uses human safety monitors in some markets. But the Cybercab is designed to operate without any human intervention, which removes one layer of safety on which Tesla can fall back. The company says it employs remote operators who can take control in case of an emergency, but experts question whether signal strength and latency could hamper reactions, especially during incidents in which every second counts. Tesla recently started adding Starlink to its Cybercabs to address this question of connectivity. There’s also the question of data, and whether Tesla has enough of the right kind. For years, Tesla was assumed to have an advantage in the race to put driverless cars on the road, thanks to the millions of vehicles on the road, passively gathering data to help train its autonomous driving models. But the Cybercab is a different type of vehicle with a unique platform that requires its own specialized data, Musk said during an earnings call in July. “We need to accumulate driving data that is specific to the Cybercab before we can put a lot of them on the road,” he said. Once considered to be a leader in data collection, Tesla may actually be a laggard. During that same earnings call, Ashok Elluswamy, the company’s head of AI, said that Tesla’s unsupervised robotaxis have driven 380,000 miles across six cities in two different states. Waymo, which has operated a commercial robotaxi service since 2020, has driven over 220 million fully driverless miles on public roads — or about 579 times more miles than Tesla. Tesla uses a mix of unsupervised and supervised vehicles as part of its current Robotaxi fleet, but that ratio appears to be in a constant state of flux. According to the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker, the company was operating 16 unsupervised vehicles in Austin, four in Dallas, and one in Houston. Tesla also hasn’t submitted its safety claims for independent analysis, instead relying on self-published statistics while actively working to block public scrutiny of the data it’s required to provide to federal regulators. Meanwhile, Waymo has published several studies in peer-reviewed journals. Recently, the nonprofit Insurance Institute for Highway Safety examined Waymo’s first 50 million miles of fully autonomous driving across multiple cities and concluded that its crash rates were significantly lower than those of human drivers. The Cybercab launch comes at an odd moment for Tesla. Whereas other vehicle launches have excited Tesla’s many fans with their cutting-edge technology, the Cybercab remains a bit of a curiosity. It’s the lightest, most efficient electric vehicle Tesla has ever produced. But it’s unclear whether the technology powering it is adequate for commercial operations. Still, it’s more like the Tesla Semi than the Model Y or Cybertruck, insofar as it seems destined for commercial service and not personal ownership — despite Musk’s claims that you will eventually be able to buy one. The Cybercab’s lack of traditional controls means it will be hamstrung by federal safety rules that require things like pedals and side mirrors before they can be sold to the public. That said, if Tesla were to receive an exemption from federal regulators, allowing the company to produce and sell thousands of Cybercabs, that calculus could change. Amazon’s Zoox recently received permission to begin charging for rides in its purpose-built robotaxi. Whether Tesla is also seeking a similar exemption is unknown. What is known is that Tesla is going to roll out the Cybercab later this month, as if it’s really ready for primetime. But lingering safety questions, as well as the limited nature of Tesla’s Robotaxi service, suggests the Cybercab may still have a long road ahead of it.

articles.summary:
Google’s Mishaal Rahman took to r/Android to announce the process, which will eventually be the only way to install apps from unverified Android developers. articles.title: This tiny, magnetic e-reader could stop you from doomscrolling
articles.summary: The Xteink X3 is a delightfully tiny, MagSafe-compatible e-ink reader that attaches to the back of your phone like a Pop Socket.
articles.body:
It was love at first sight. It felt like scouring the mall, dipping in and out of sprawling department stores in search of a specific, elusive item, only to finally find what you’re looking for. Only, I didn’t even know I was searching for something like the Xteink X3 , because I never dared dream of something so delightful: a tiny, MagSafe-compatible e-ink reader that could attach to my iPhone like a Pop Socket.

This was it. My life would change forever. I would get my hands on the Xteink X3, and I would stop doomscrolling forever. I would read more books than ever before… which is saying something, since — brag — I read at least 50 books a year. But — not a brag — I probably spend even more time on social media than I do reading. I know that I feel generally less anxious when I limit my social media time, but alas, the siren song of TikTok beckons me. What if instead of opening social media, I could just flip my phone over and read on a tiny, Kindle-like e-ink screen? Could this $80 gadget fix me?

Since we first published this review in May, Xteink released the X4 Pro, which adds a touchscreen and a front light. Find out what I thought of it here . It’s $99 from Xteink’s website , while the older model is now discounted to $69 at Amazon .

I’ve tried reading books (… or downloads from AO3 ) on my phone, immersing myself in a fictional world, rather than posts from the president in which he threatens to obliterate an entire country . But something about looking at my phone, where I’m constantly tempted to open Instagram to see whatever Reel someone sent me, doesn’t quite soothe me the way that a book or an e-ink device like a Kindle does.

I was so excited for my X3 to arrive that I constantly refreshed the tracking link until finally, it was delivered. Even though I had meticulously compared the dimensions of the X3 to my iPhone 16, or my Pop Socket wallet, I still worried it might not fit — the previous model, the Xteink X4 (basically the same device but a little bigger) only fit on larger phones like the iPhone Pro Max line. But sure enough, the X3 magnetically attached to the back of my phone like it was custom-made to fit.

My X3 came in the mail about two hours before I had to leave to go to a Phillies game, so I rushed to load books onto it, because I thought it would be really funny to take photos in which I read “The Power Broker” in a crowded baseball stadium. Behold, my handiwork:

For the first several days that I had the X3, I carried it with me on the back of my phone. This made me a bit nervous, though, since I’m used to having a Pop Socket wallet, which means I’ve gotten in the habit of leaving home without my actual wallet. But I found that I used the X3 just as much when I carried it in my purse or pocket, rather than attaching it to my phone. I’m still not sure if I’ll keep this setup, or if I’ll start actually using a real wallet so that I can attach the e-reader, but for now, that’s what has felt most natural. Plus, my X3 shipped with a very compact, cute, magnetic case, which perfectly protects the device and its screen and makes it a little easier to hold. At just $9 for the case, I’d recommend getting one. The case can also magnetize to your phone, though it feels a bit less secure than attaching your X3 alone.

Over my two weeks of testing, I did find that the X3 helped me read more. If you’re in line at a coffee shop, or waiting for the bus, you can just pull out the e-reader instead of opening Instagram. I didn’t find the small screen difficult to read on, either. But just buying the device won’t change your habits — you have to remember that you have a 3.7-inch screen in your pocket that can fit hundreds of books.

The Xteink X3 is pretty close to being the device of my dreams, but it’s not quite there yet. The firmware that the device comes with is pretty clunky — not unusable, but not exactly intuitive. I expected this, since the Xteink Reddit community was buzzing about CrossPoint , a community-made, free, open source firmware. The process of downloading CrossPoint was a bit intimidating as someone who writes words, rather than code — but with the instructions on CrossPoint’s website (and a few videos), it was easy enough. I encountered some difficulties at first, but then I realized it was because I was trying to download the X4 firmware onto my X3, so… my bad. You probably won’t even need the YouTube videos!

When you start loading books and open source firmware onto your X3, you’ll notice another divisive aspect of the device: It doesn’t have a USB-C port, unlike the X4. Instead, it uses a magnetic charger. Yes, it’s annoying to have yet another charging cable specifically for this one device, but I don’t care that much. After two weeks of consistent use, my X3 has dropped from a 100% charge to a 96% charge, so I can’t imagine I’ll be using that magnetic charger too often. You don’t even need the cord to add new books to your e-reader — you can transfer files over Wi-Fi from your phone or computer (I wouldn’t call the process user-friendly, but I was able to figure it out without Googling anything).

Speaking of loading books, that’s another drawback. The majority of what I read on my Kindle comes from Libby, which is my favorite app (#notsponsored). The Libby app allows you to easily borrow e-books or audiobooks from your library and send them to your Kindle. But you can’t get those e-books (legally) onto an Xteink e-reader, since libraries use protected versions of .epub files that deter users from copying them (you also can’t read books you buy from Amazon’s e-book store on non-Amazon devices, because capitalism). This lack of compatibility is a drawback, but it also makes the device feel unique — it’s a “dumb” device that has no apps and no touch screen, which feels startlingly refreshing in an era of AI-enabled refrigerators.

It’s not hard to find interesting .epub files to load onto the X3, even if you can’t access your Kindle library or Libby. A lot of great books are in the public domain, which means that they’re no longer subject to copyright and can be downloaded for free (I’ve weirdly never read “Pride and Prejudice,” so the time is now). A few months ago, I bought the entire .epub catalogs of sci-fi writers Charlie Jane Anders and Annalee Newitz as part of a charity fundraiser, which should keep me busy for quite a bit. If you wanted to, you could even turn online articles or blogs into .epubs using a free program like Calibre .

So, did the Xteink X3 fix me? Am I now a newly reformed woman who has a healthy relationship with social media and has read a bunch of classic novels that I never read as an English major, since I mostly took classes with ridiculous titles like “Aestheticus Extremus: The Politics of Precarious Invention in North American Poetry and Poetics”? It’s not that simple. But if you meet the X3 halfway and make a concerted effort to use it, then maybe you’ll spare yourself from a bit more brain rot.

This post originally published May 3 and has since been updated to reflect updated pricing and discounts.

articles.title: Let’s take a look at the retro tech making a comeback | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Boom boxes, instant cameras, and even landlines are making a comeback. Here are the coolest retro-inspired devices available.
articles.body:
From blasting music on a boom box to watching a photo develop in your hands, many people are rediscovering the imperfect charm of older gadgets that smartphones and laptops just can’t replicate.

Tech companies are leaning all the way in, blending nostalgic design with modern functionality. Here are some of the coolest retro-inspired devices out there right now.

In a world full of endless notifications, tabs, doomscrolling, and other distractions, smart typewriters are carving out a niche for a more focused writing experience. These devices strip things back to the essentials: just you, a keyboard, and your words.

Freewrite ( $699 ): Freewrite features a design inspired by classic typewriters, providing a minimalist writing experience. It includes a small screen and satisfying keys to press. However, if you need to make edits, your drafts are synced to the cloud and can be exported to any software.

Pomera ($549): A more modern take than Freewrite’s device, Pomera looks like a compact laptop and includes helpful tools like spell check, document management, and word counts. With multiple transfer options and up to 20 hours of battery life, it balances simplicity with functionality.

Boom boxes, cassette tapes, and record players

The boom box is re-emerging as both a design statement and a functional audio device. Today’s versions pair chunky buttons, cassette decks, and oversized speakers with modern upgrades like Bluetooth and rechargeable batteries. Cassette players, meanwhile, are also reappearing with enhancements, and record players continue to be popular as well.

We Are Rewind ($525): A modern reimagining of the classic boom box, the GB-001 has everything you desire in a boom box, but better. It keeps all the essential features, such as woofers, tweeters, a cassette player, and recorder, while adding Bluetooth and a rechargeable battery. With speakers delivering 104 W of power, it’s built for both nostalgia and high-quality sound.

Bumpboxx : Now live on Kickstarter, the new BB-777 is a portable boom box that has a bold ’80s aesthetic while packing in a wide range of features. It includes a powerful three-way speaker system, dual cassette decks with recording and high-speed dubbing, a built-in CD player, USB recording, and more. It also supports multiband radio, including AM and FM.

Retrospekt ($99): A minimalist take on the classic Walkman-style player, this portable cassette device features all the essentials: play, rewind, fast-forward, and record. It supports both battery power and USB-C, making it a simple but modern throwback.

Kickback World ($500): This DEKO record player started shipping in January 2025 and has become popular not just for being a step up from traditional players, but also for aesthetic appeal with its orange acrylic, “Swedish modernism” design compared to the traditional, suitcase-style record players we normally see.

There’s something uniquely satisfying about holding a physical photo seconds after taking it. That sense of excitement and anticipation, combined with the imperfect beauty of film, makes each shot feel more meaningful than a quick snap on your iPhone.

Polaroid ($249) : Polaroid has never stopped being popular, but it’s always innovating. Most recently, the Polaroid Flip launched last year, a retro-looking instant camera with modern features like autofocus and app connectivity for remote control.

Fujifilm ($225) : If you want a hybrid camera that lets you shoot digitally and print photos, then there’s the Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo . It offers the best of both worlds: instant film with the flexibility of digital storage and sharing. In recent years, the device received an upgrade with USB-C. In January, Fujifilm launched a new variant, the Instax Mini Evo Cinema ($412) , a three-in-one hybrid camera that can even print images from your smartphone.

Kodak ($30) : You also can’t go wrong with a classic single-use, disposable camera. It’s simple, reliable, and still delivers quality photos without needing any photography skills. Last year, Kodak released a miniature keychain digital camera, the “Charmera.” A twist on its signature “Fling” camera, this tiny device can save and transfer photos and videos using a USB-C cable.

Landline phones are making a quiet comeback, especially among people seeking a break from screen-heavy communication. They’re also gaining popularity as aesthetic objects, often used as statement pieces in home décor.

Tin Can ($100): Remember the days when you would rush home after school to use the landline and chat with your friends for hours? That’s the inspiration behind Tin Can. Designed for kids, it resembles a landline phone but doesn’t require a phone jack, just Wi-Fi. Only approved people can call, and parents can easily manage contacts through a companion app. You can preorder now. There’s a free plan to call other Tin Can users and a $9.99/month plan for calling all approved contacts.

paragraphs: From blasting music on a boom box to watching a photo develop in your hands, many people are rediscovering the imperfect charm of older gadgets that smartphones and laptops just can’t replicate.
Tech companies are leaning all the way in, blending nostalgic design with modern functionality. Here are some of the coolest retro-inspired devices out there right now.

In a world full of endless notifications, tabs, doomscrolling, and other distractions, smart typewriters are carving out a niche for a more focused writing experience. These devices strip things back to the essentials: just you, a keyboard, and your words.

Freewrite ( $699 ): Freewrite features a design inspired by classic typewriters, providing a minimalist writing experience. It includes a small screen and satisfying keys to press. However, if you need to make edits, your drafts are synced to the cloud and can be exported to any software.

Pomera ($549): A more modern take than Freewrite’s device, Pomera looks like a compact laptop and includes helpful tools like spell check, document management, and word counts. With multiple transfer options and up to 20 hours of battery life, it balances simplicity with functionality.
Boom boxes, cassette tapes, and record players

The boom box is re-emerging as both a design statement and a functional audio device. Today’s versions pair chunky buttons, cassette decks, and oversized speakers with modern upgrades like Bluetooth and rechargeable batteries. Cassette players, meanwhile, are also reappearing with enhancements, and record players continue to be popular as well.

We Are Rewind ($525): A modern reimagining of the classic boom box, the GB-001 has everything you desire in a boom box, but better. It keeps all the essential features, such as woofers, tweeters, a cassette player, and recorder, while adding Bluetooth and a rechargeable battery. With speakers delivering 104 W of power, it’s built for both nostalgia and high-quality sound.

Bumpboxx : Now live on Kickstarter, the new BB-777 is a portable boom box that has a bold ’80s aesthetic while packing in a wide range of features. It includes a powerful three-way speaker system, dual cassette decks with recording and high-speed dubbing, a built-in CD player, USB recording, and more. It also supports multiband radio, including AM and FM.

Retrospekt ($99): A minimalist take on the classic Walkman-style player, this portable cassette device features all the essentials: play, rewind, fast-forward, and record. It supports both battery power and USB-C, making it a simple but modern throwback.

Kickback World ($500): This DEKO record player started shipping in January 2025 and has become popular not just for being a step up from traditional players, but also for aesthetic appeal with its orange acrylic, “Swedish modernism” design compared to the traditional, suitcase-style record players we normally see.

There’s something uniquely satisfying about holding a physical photo seconds after taking it. That sense of excitement and anticipation, combined with the imperfect beauty of film, makes each shot feel more meaningful than a quick snap on your iPhone.

Polaroid ($249) : Polaroid has never stopped being popular, but it’s always innovating. Most recently, the Polaroid Flip launched last year, a retro-looking instant camera with modern features like autofocus and app connectivity for remote control.

Fujifilm ($225) : If you want a hybrid camera that lets you shoot digitally and print photos, then there’s the Fujifilm Instax Mini Evo . It offers the best of both worlds: instant film with the flexibility of digital storage and sharing. In recent years, the device received an upgrade with USB-C. In January, Fujifilm launched a new variant, the Instax Mini Evo Cinema ($412) , a three-in-one hybrid camera that can even print images from your smartphone.

Kodak ($30) : You also can’t go wrong with a classic single-use, disposable camera. It’s simple, reliable, and still delivers quality photos without needing any photography skills. Last year, Kodak released a miniature keychain digital camera, the “Charmera.” A twist on its signature “Fling” camera, this tiny device can save and transfer photos and videos using a USB-C cable.

Landline phones are making a quiet comeback, especially among people seeking a break from screen-heavy communication. They’re also gaining popularity as aesthetic objects, often used as statement pieces in home décor.

Tin Can ($100): Remember the days when you would rush home after school to use the landline and chat with your friends for hours? That’s the inspiration behind Tin Can. Designed for kids, it resembles a landline phone but doesn’t require a phone jack, just Wi-Fi. Only approved people can call, and parents can easily manage contacts through a companion app. You can preorder now. There’s a free plan to call other Tin Can users and a $9.99/month plan for calling all approved contacts.

Clicks ($499): Announced at CES 2026 , hardware company Clicks Technology debuted its smartphone that looks a lot like a BlackBerry, which dominated the phone market back in the 2000s and has seen a revival among Gen Z. While Clicks’ phone has access to text messaging and productivity apps like Gmail and Slack, it doesn’t provide access to mobile games and social media, making it an enticing alternative for people looking to go back to the good old days.

articles.title: Google’s Pixel Watch 5 is promising — but it isn’t finished
articles.summary: The $399.99 Google Pixel Watch 5
articles.body: The Google Pixel Watch 5 has, in many ways, been the hardest Pixel Watch to accurately review. Barely anything has changed in terms of hardware. The sizes are the same, the chips and battery got an itty-bitty boost, and there’s a new pyrite satin case finish. Instead, the big updates are all software-related: This year’s watch gets ambitious new health features that expand on the overhauled Google Health app and its AI coach introduced with the Fitbit Air earlier this year. The only problem is those health updates aren’t here. The watch’s most interesting new features — blood pressure and insulin resistance trends, nightly sleep breathing quality, and strength training cues from the wrist — won’t start rolling out until next month. And in the case of breathing emergency detection, which calls emergency services if the device detects you’ve stopped breathing, the feature is still pending FDA clearance. (Europe will get it at launch, but this isn’t the sort of feature you can test anyway.)  That leaves me and the Pixel Watch 5 on my wrist in a bit of a reviewer’s pickle. All those features sound smart to me, but I can’t weigh in on whether they’re worth $399.99 — a $50 price hike over last year’s model — until they’re available. Given that half of those new metrics are meant to be viewed monthly, it’ll be a hot minute before I can write about them. [Product: Google Pixel Watch 5 | https://www.amazon.com/Google-Pixel-Watch-41mm-Smartwatch/dp/B0H7WX3DCB?tag=theverge02-20, https://www.anrdoezrs.net/links/8836598/type/dlg/https://store.google.com/product/pixel_watch_5?hl=en-US, https://bestbuy.7tiv.net/c/482924/614286/10014?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.bestbuy.com%2Fproduct%2Fgoogle-pixel-watch-5-41mm-wi-fi-matte-black-case-obsidian-band-2026%2FJ39TC82RLZ%2Fsku%2F6686031] Which leaves the rest of the Pixel Watch 5 software updates: Wear OS 7, offline Gemini, a more accurate Raise to Talk feature, Proactive Assistance, more integrated gesture controls in the UI, AI watchfaces, some improved bedtime automations, and better GPS maps for outdoor activities. Broadly, I get the vibe Google’s going for — subtly helpful AI that enables glanceable, quickly actionable information — and I like it. However, except for GPS, these are refinements. They’re not mind-blowing updates that warrant morphing into the “Shut up and take my money!” meme. At launch, these will be exclusive to the Pixel Watch 5, but Google does have a history of software updates trickling down to older models with time. Wear OS 7 isn’t a major departure from Wear OS 6. The double pinch and wrist turn gestures are now more directly integrated into the UI. At certain points (e.g., scrolling or selecting), you’ll see an animated chip of the pinching gesture. It’s a handy way of teaching you when a gesture can be used. During “live” activities — say, a workout or timer — another chip will appear on the main watchface. Flipping your wrist will dismiss your current screen or a call. These aren’t unique ideas. The Apple Watch has had them for a while. However, I love that they’re more prominently featured on the Pixel Watch (and not just the Watch 5). You’ll never see me pooh-pooh well-executed gesture controls on smartwatches simply because they’re not 100 percent new. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review7.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I was less enamored with Proactive Assistance. As my colleagues Dom Preston, David Imel, and Cameron Faulkner have noted in their Pixel 11 reviews, these Gemini-powered suggestions don’t always work as intended. You may also never notice them! On the watch, it was helpful when a friend texted me via Google Messages about my availability for plans. A chip for my Google Calendar instantly popped up. Except those were orchestrated scenarios for testing. In real life, I mostly plan hangouts over Slack or phone calls, where Gemini isn’t integrated. I get the concept, and I can see this improving with future updates. But for now your mileage will vary. Offline Gemini was more convenient in testing than I’d anticipated. I had zero intention of running with the Pixel 11 Pro Fold that I’d paired with my Watch 5. I’ve dropped way too many a smartphone to risk wrecking a caseless, $1,900 phone. Nevertheless, Gemini was able to start a workout via voice command, as well as quickly obtain a GPS signal well out of Bluetooth range of the phone, and therefore internet. (I did this exact testing scenario before setting up cellular.) There’s still some latency when you use wrist-based Gemini — offline or otherwise — but not so egregious that it’s unusable. Especially for basic tasks. Speaking of GPS, I called Google bold when it claimed the GPS on the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms that on the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fenix 8 Pro. It does this by utilizing 3D models of buildings, weather data, dual-frequency GPS, and other sensor signals to “correct” wonky GPS data after an activity. When I poked and prodded Google’s Pixel Watch reps at my demos, they didn’t flinch. There was no hedging, no caveats. Just a “we tested it in Manhattan, a GPS nightmare, go forth, Vee, and run till your little legs give out” kind of confidence. I still have a lot more GPS testing I want to do (different terrains, durations, and outdoor exercises), but I have to say — the GPS is dramatically improved, and it outperformed the Ultra 3 in my testing. To test the GPS, I recorded three separate 20-to-30-minute walks in the West Village in Manhattan. During each of these walks, I walked in zigzags, annoyed cabbies by jaywalking across streets I wasn’t supposed to, and annoyed a friend by walking literal circles around her. As you can see in the screenshots here, the Ultra 3 overcorrected, so it appears like I’m mostly walking in a straight line. The Pixel Watch 5 didn’t catch all of my tests — but it did accurately register some of my zigzags, instances where I doubled back on purpose, and one time where I circled my friend. (I currently don’t have a Garmin Fenix 8 Pro, so I wasn’t able to compare it to that device, though you can check out DC Rainmaker’s more hardcore Pixel Watch 5 GPS tests here.)  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Screenshot_20260819-085714.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2340.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Screenshot_20260819-090305.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2341.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Screenshot_20260819-090316.png?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/IMG_2342.png?quality=90&strip=all] I doubt most Garmin or Ultra 3 fans will be enticed to switch based on improved GPS alone. I mean, the Pixel Watch’s design still doesn’t scream rugged durability — something most outdoor enthusiasts like. This is more Google leaning into its strengths to deliver a clever solution to a long-standing problem with Pixel and Fitbit wearables. I wouldn’t say it’s perfect. No GPS tracking is. It’s more that GPS accuracy is no longer a reason to hold back from getting a Pixel Watch if you want one. Which leaves me to regale you with the most bizarre feature I tested: AI watchfaces.  I get why Google made this feature. It acknowledges that there’s a contingent of smartwatch fans who want as many watchfaces as possible and don’t want to rely on a company’s artistic curation. (Cough, Apple.) Theoretically, prompting an AI to generate a watchface of your specific idea makes sense.  But this is also AI. See: this incredibly dooftastic AI-generated watchface of a manta ray. This is not a manta ray. This is number-shaped blobs with eyes and cartoony dinosaur fins.  [Image: Pray tell, in what world is THIS a manta ray? It’s cute! It’s just not a manta ray! https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review11.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I had more success asking for a cute Kirby-inspired watchface with “a playful font in a pink and purple theme.” Is it a tad unsettling that these are, again, Kirby-shaped numbers and Kirby’s face plastered onto them? Yeah, but it works. I had the most success with a cross-stitch-themed watchface featuring “fat and cute forest creatures and a retro font.” Sure, portions of the numbers are an embroidered satin stitch and not cross-stitches, but the spirit is there. My main gripe is how limited the customization is. You can tweak the appearance of the clock numbers, colors, and font, and choose one of three basic layouts, but little else. Is this a feature worth boiling oceans for? No, but it’s whimsical enough to please the people it’s intended for. The hardware tweaks this year aren’t that noticeable. Swiping through screens is snappy but not radically improved. Like its predecessor, the 45mm Watch 5 lasted roughly 36 to 40 hours on a single charge in testing. A year later, I still like the watch stand charger. Fast charging is good enough that you can stick it on the charger while you shower and make it through the day (or night).  [Image: This prompt was not a keeper. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/google_pixel_watch_5_review3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Right now, I feel comfortable saying the Pixel Watch 5 is a great Android smartwatch. RIP OnePlus, and Samsung has been coasting since the Galaxy Watch 6. So, like last year, this is the Android smartwatch to beat. It’s the one I’d recommend to Android smartwatch newcomers, and the $50 price hike thanks to RAMageddon isn’t as bad as it could’ve been.  If you’re an owner of a recent Pixel Watch, I don’t think this is the year to upgrade, though. And even if you’ve got a Pixel Watch 2 or earlier, I’d still wait until the new health features are out and tested before buying. Alternatively, you could opt for doubling up with a Fitbit Air instead of a new watch if you’re mainly annoyed about having to charge frequently for sleep tracking. I don’t love feeling like a review is unfinished, but alas — that’s how it is this year. See you back in October for part two after the rest of the health features drop.  Photography by Victoria Song / The Verge --- Agree to Continue: Google Pixel Watch 5 Every smart device now requires you to agree to a series of terms and conditions before you can use it — contracts that no one actually reads. It’s impossible for us to read and analyze every single one of these agreements. But we started counting exactly how many times you have to hit “agree” to use devices when we review them, since these are agreements most people don’t read and definitely can’t negotiate. To use the Google Pixel Watch 5, you must pair it with an Android smartphone. That includes the phone’s Terms of Service, privacy policy, and any other permissions you grant, such as Bluetooth access and location services. You may also want to familiarize yourself with settings regarding opting in or out of your health data being used for AI training. Integrating other third-party health APIs (e.g., connecting to Strava) means you’re also agreeing to each service’s terms and privacy policy. By setting up the Google Pixel Watch 5, you’re agreeing to: * Google Terms of Service * Google Play Terms of Service * Google Privacy Policy (included in Terms of Service) * Google Health Additional Terms of Service * Google Health Data and Privacy Policy (formerly Fitbit) Final tally: Five mandatory policies and several optional permissions. ---

articles.title: Waymo lifts the lid on the ‘brain’ powering its robotaxis
articles.summary: Waymo, for the first time, revealed key details about the compute system and hardware used to power its fleet of driverless vehicles.
articles.body: What’s in the trunk of your car? Shopping bags? A spare tire? Jumper cables? What about a high-powered computer capable of performing up to one quadrillion operations a second? Only if you’re Waymo. For the first time, Waymo revealed key details about the heavy compute “brain” housed in the trunk of its robotaxis, including chip architecture, processor specs, and internal component details. The details, published in a blog post today, also includes a list of hardware suppliers that Waymo uses to build the computers that power its driverless fleet. It’s a revealing look at the world’s leading player in driverless technology. Waymo is currently operating around 4,000 vehicles in over 10 cities, conducting approximately 500,000 paid trips a week. The company claims that its technology significantly reduces traffic crashes and injuries as compared to human drivers. And while a lot of the work to run its vehicles relies on heavy training and simulation that runs in the cloud, a good portion also takes place in the vehicles themselves. Waymo’s robotaxis, festooned with cameras, lidar, and radar, take in massive streams of raw sensor data. That data is processed by artificial intelligence to instantly understand what’s happening around the car, turning that information into safe driving commands in milliseconds. Its computers, which are installed in the trunks of its vehicles, are built to act like its eyes, ears, and brain, to process a full 360-degree view and make split-second decisions without any human backup. [Image: Waymo’s compute needs to run silently while also not taking up too much room in the trunk. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Compute-Image-1.png?quality=90&strip=all] “Compute systems for autonomous driving handle highly diverse workloads,” Satish Jeyachandran, VP of Engineering, and Daniel Rosenband, Compute Lead, write in the blog post. “At Waymo, we are designing a state-of-the-art system that would be considered impressive for a data center, with the added complexity of an in-vehicle operating domain and real-time requirements.” Jeyachandran and Rosenband describe three core principles guiding the design of its compute: responsive, ruggedized, and redundant. The stack needs to be able to respond to sensor data as quickly and with as little latency as possible. This requires massive amounts of compute power, which Waymo has scaled 20 times in the past eight years. It also needs to be able to handle all the bumps and cracks in the road, as well as extreme temperatures. And it basically needs to be able to run two systems in parallel, in the event that one fails. These three principles are “non-negotiable,” the executives write. It also needs to not take up the entire trunk. After all, there are passengers and their luggage to consider. And it needs to run nearly silent, so as not to compromise the rider experience. And while Waymo builds its compute stack itself, it also relies on a network of third-party suppliers to provide the components it can’t build itself. Waymo’s effort to explain how its multi-sensor system can fuse data in real time is especially noteworthy considering Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s dismissal of these systems as inherently faulty. Musk has called lidar a “crutch” and “a fool’s errand,” arguing that sensor fusion between cameras, radar, and lidar introduces dangerous “sensor contention.” He also contends that when differing sensor data disagree, figuring out which signal to trust creates deadly ambiguity rather than safety. But Waymo argues that its robust and redundant system is what enables it to deploy its vehicles at scale. “We built an [machine learning]-primary architecture to run advanced neural networks at minimal latency,” the executives write. “To manage critical non-ML tasks like orchestration, data movement, and logging while maximizing time for ML computation, we pair our ML technologies with the best CPUs, GPUs, and accelerators. The result is a balanced, heterogeneous system.” [Image: Waymo’s custom 5nm ASCI handles the massive firehouse of incoming data from its sensors. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Compute-Image-3.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] In the blog post, Waymo introduces its custom silicon chip, a 5-nanometer ASIC, built to handle the massive firehose of incoming data from its sensors. Instead of sending raw, messy data straight to the car’s main brain, the chip sits at the front lines cleaning up the data, combining the sensor inputs, and running fast AI checks right as the information comes in. The chip’s dedicated front-end processing provides 1,000 TOPS (trillion operations a second). And because it was built specifically for Waymo’s autonomous driving operations, it fits neatly in the overall stack, helping keep reaction times minimal. Consider this scene below. Waymo’s executives claim its system can more quickly process high-fidelity data from its 13 high-res cameras “simultaneously and in real-time” to deliver improved low-light perception. In that way, it can see a lot more stuff in the dark (the image on the right) that traditional cameras often miss (the image on the left). [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/Compute-Image-4.png?quality=90&strip=all] Jeyachandran and Rosenband conclude the blog post by running through a list of hardware suppliers who are helping build Waymo’s cutting edge system: AMD, Micron, Nvidia, Samsung, SanDisk, Socionext, and TSMC. Rather than try to build its own compute system from scratch, the company is instead focusing its internal efforts on real-time sensor fusion and front-end machine learning, while leaning on the global supply chain for everything else. It’s a revealing glimpse of the technology that Waymo uses to power its fleet of robotaxis. But the company doesn’t get into one important aspect: How much does all this cost? Some estimates put it at $20,000 to $25,000 per vehicle for its sixth-generation hardware. While that’s a huge decrease from the fifth-generation’s estimated cost of $100,000 to $125,000 per vehicle, it still shows how Waymo’s continued expansion could be hampered by high hardware expenses. Building a brain to run an entire fleet of driverless cars is a monumental achievement, no question. But building a business that can make a profit is another challenge altogether.

articles.title: Tesla Robotaxis appear to go fully unsupervised in Austin ahead of Cybercab launch
articles.summary: Tesla’s Robotaxis in Austin appear to be fully unsupervised ahead of the company’s Cybercab launch, according to the creator of a crowdsourced tracking website.
articles.body: Seven months after Elon Musk announced that Tesla Robotaxis in Austin were operating without human safety monitors onboard, the city’s service appears to have finally gone fully driverless. Over the past two weeks, all 170 Tesla Robotaxi rides in Austin monitored by the crowdsourced Robotaxi Tracker were unsupervised, the site’s creator, Ethan McKanna, told The Verge. Those rides involved 54 different cars. McKanna has also seen a sharp increase in unsupervised Robotaxis elsewhere, particularly Dallas and Houston, where roughly 30 driverless Teslas have been operating over the past week.  That’s a substantial change from earlier this summer, when Tesla’s unsupervised fleet appeared to be stagnating or even shrinking. Robotaxi Tracker showed just 28 active unsupervised vehicles across six Texas and Florida markets as recently as last week. In other words, McKanna has now identified nearly twice as many unsupervised Teslas in Austin alone as his tracker had previously shown across all six markets. Some of the apparent jump reflects better data. McKanna, who spent this summer interning with Tesla’s Robotaxi team, said some of the metrics on his site had been lagging. After revising the sources feeding Robotaxi Tracker — which draws primarily on app users automatically logging their rides, along with other crowdsourced and public information — he found that more vehicles were operating unsupervised than the site had previously reflected. He’s currently updating the site to incorporate the revised data. But the Austin shift itself appears to be real. “Austin has seemingly stopped supervised rides for a couple weeks now,” McKanna said. “Plates previously marked as supervised have been confirmed to be offering unsupervised rides.” The site’s findings also corroborate what some Robotaxi users in the Austin area have recently reported on Reddit and X. McKanna’s site is one of the few ways to track the makeup of Tesla’s Robotaxi fleet, since Tesla does not publish detailed fleet data and typically does not respond to press inquiries. Tesla did not respond to requests for comment for this article. The shift comes as Tesla prepares to launch the Cybercab, its purpose-built robotaxi, in Austin as soon as this month. Unlike the Model Ys currently providing rides, Cybercabs are designed without traditional controls such as a steering wheel or pedals, making Tesla’s ability to operate vehicles without onboard monitors particularly important to the Cybercab rollout. On Tesla’s most recent earnings call, Musk said the Robotaxi program would scale “very, very rapidly,” but offered no new target for how many vehicles or cities Tesla would reach — a departure from the much more specific robotaxi forecasts he has repeatedly missed. Tesla may also be limiting the number of Model Ys it adds as it prepares for Cybercab. According to a new JPMorgan note, Tesla is intentionally holding back on adding Model Ys to the Robotaxi fleet because it expects to scale Cybercab in the near term. Even after the jump in unsupervised Robotaxis, Tesla remains far behind its biggest robotaxi competitor. Waymo operates more than 300 driverless vehicles in Austin alone, and has around 4,000 vehicles across 10 other cities.

articles.title: Amazon’s drone deliveries are landing in pools and ponds
articles.summary: Amazon’s Prime Air drones have dropped deliveries into water a few times over the past year, with the latest incident showing a drone dropping a package directly into a pool.
articles.body: Amazon’s speedy drone delivery service will soon reach 500 cities across the US — but that might just mean there are more pools to drop packages into. On Wednesday, ABC7 News Bay Area shared a video showing an Amazon delivery drone hovering over a customer’s pool in Texas, before opening its hatch and plopping the package directly into the water. This isn’t the first time Amazon’s drones have delivered soggy packages. A video shared last July shows a Prime Air drone dropping a package right next to a customer’s pool in Arizona, but air sent downward by the drone’s propellers blew it straight into the water. In an interview with local news outlet AZFamily 3TV at the time, the customer said he let Amazon choose the delivery location for him. Another incident from May shows an Amazon drone dropping a package near a pond, which bounces off the ground and tumbles into the water. [Media: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cjMC696W-Ek] Last year, Amazon halted drone deliveries in the West Valley Phoenix Metro Area when two of its MK30 drones crashed into a crane. Its drones have also been spotted cutting an internet cable and colliding with an apartment building. Amazon says that once its drones reach the delivery point, “it will check to confirm there are no people, pets, or vehicles in the way before safely delivering the package.” Maybe it needs to check for water, too. Amazon didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
